Castle grew up close to Atlanta but declined to work out for the Hawks—who had the number one pick in the 2024 draft—partly to avoid getting relegated to off-ball duties alongside his hometown team’s then centerpiece Trae Young. Instead, after winning a national championship as a freshman playing for the famously merciless coach Dan Hurley at the University of Connecticut, he went fourth, to the Spurs.

Harper and Castle attended basketball camps and games alongside other high-level prospects, quietly orbiting each other but never colliding, until Castle dunked on Harper during Harper’s very first day of practice with the Spurs. At another early practice, it happened again. An errant shot caromed off the rim, and he went to grab the rebound.

“You dunked on me off a putback,” Harper says. “You counting that?” Castle just nods.

Goldsberry goes further: “When you have three dudes who could all be First Team All-NBA, and they’re all 22 or under—I mean, who wouldn’t be confident?”

“I’m going to win Sixth Man of the Year this year,” he says.
“No you’re not, bro,” Castle scoffs.

“You’re not going to be Sixth Man,” Castle says. “Who are you going to be Sixth Man for?”

Fox has eagerly taken on the role of mentoring the young guards even though their ascension may come at the cost of his starting job. “I’m not worried about it at all,” the nine-year NBA vet says. “That’s not my decision to make. I go in, I control what I can control, and try to help put us in the best position to win.”

In Castle and Harper, you can see the early outlines of an all-time NBA pairing. “Even if Victor Wembanyama vanished,” Goldsberry says, “the Spurs, having these two dudes, still have one of the brightest futures in the league.”

Defining those early contours requires not just sorting out roles but also figuring out everything else that comes with being a star player in the league. The outfits, of course, have become increasingly essential. So much so that before a Finals game in New York, Harper and teammate Carter Bryant went shopping for outfits to wear to the game the next day. “We definitely went to Balenciaga, got a bunch of shit,” Harper says.

Despite playing until mid-June in the Finals, the two have already filled their calendars back up with basketball activities. Harper says it took his body weeks to feel normal again after the long playoff run, but lately he’s been working out, running stairs in Santa Barbara. He’ll head to Turks and Caicos this weekend with his brother—Celtics wing Ron Harper Jr.— while other teammates go to practice with Fox in Houston. In late July, they’ll travel to Paris for a Wembanyama-organized hangout that’s about as mandatory as an unofficial team event can be. “You want that max [contract extension] next year, you’ll be there,” Harper tells Castle, when the latter says he doesn’t have to attend.

Harper is already scheduled to be back in San Antonio for two weeks at the start of August. “They got you on that rookie plan,” Castle observes. Before long, training camp will ramp up. Another season, another shot for the two guards to meet their goals: to make the All-Star and All-Defensive teams, Castle says, and—they both say this nearly simultaneously—“Win a championship.”

“I’m over it,” Harper says of the Finals. “You over it?” he turns to ask Castle.

When I ask if any moments from the series still haunt him, Harper fishes his phone out of his pocket to revisit one of the most painful beats, just to prove how over it he is: OG Anunoby’s tip-in from Game 4, which capped off a 29-point Knicks comeback, the largest in Finals history. As a fan, even a month later, watching this is like watching a character wander into the basement in a horror movie; I want to yell at him to stop.

As the Knicks dug their way out of the hole, Harper and Castle could feel the floor of Madison Square Garden quaking underneath their feet. “That’s the loudest I’ve ever heard an arena,” Harper says, scrubbing through an Instagram clip. He eventually finds the angle he’s looking for and points to his reaction under the basket, the O of his mouth growing in slow motion.

“No,” Castle says, turning away, “I don’t be watching that shit, bro.”
“I got to watch it, bro. It happened,” Harper says.
It took Harper several weeks to wash the taste of the Finals loss out of his mouth, but it got easier when he restarted his workouts. “It helps me work out harder,” he says.

Every great team in NBA history has painful playoff series on their résumés; it’s a credit to this Spurs squad that theirs just happened to come in the Finals. Castle and Harper have put the loss behind them—“Just for the offseason, I’m over it,” Harper says—but they’re trying to take the necessary lessons from it, too. “I don’t think it’s like, ‘Oh shit, we made it there, it’s easy,’ ” Harper says. “It’s more that we understand what goes into [making] it. Now, we got to do it.”
I ask them to project out over the next five years. How many Finals appearances do they envision? “Hopefully five,” Harper says. “I mean, that’s the goal.”
Castle finishes his backcourt partner’s thought one more time: “We finna go back.”

Harper finishes, catching the lob: “And it’ll be like 15 of us playing that shit.” (Werewolf, which is billed as “a party game for devious people,” was a big hit.)

On the road during the season, the Spurs do activities together and always make sure to celebrate a teammate’s birthday. “Remember Houston, when Vic went off?” Castle says, jogging Harper’s memory of a particularly epic night. After beating the Rockets in a late-January matchup during the slog of the season right before the All-Star break, the team went to dinner, then ended up at some after-hours spot, where Wembanyama—whom Castle describes as a goofy, “regular-ass 22-year-old”—fully let loose alongside the rest of the team, according to the two guards.

“First time ever, probably,” Harper says. “And then we lost to Charlotte the next game. We all learned our lesson.” But in a league where team chemistry can make all the difference, maybe a few regular-season wins are worth trading for boosts in camaraderie.

The history of the NBA is full of teams that peaked too early. An unexpected loss to the Houston Rockets in the ’95 Finals should have been only a speed bump for Penny Hardaway and Shaq’s Orlando Magic on the way to many titles; the Oklahoma City Thunder, blessed with three future MVPs in Kevin Durant, James Harden, and Russell Westbrook, was supposed to be booking a timeshare in the Finals even after losing to the Heat in 2012. Neither of those teams made it back.

But Johnson believes his team has something unique in the Castle-Harper pairing. “To have two young men, with the talent and the potential and the future that’s right ahead of them, not only complement one another and be happy for one another, but to really, truly celebrate each other’s success—I’ve never experienced anything like it,” he says.

Goldsberry goes further: “When you have three dudes who could all be First Team All-NBA, and they’re all 22 or under—I mean, who wouldn’t be confident?”

When I conjure the ghost of would-be dynasties past, Harper and Castle both assert that this Spurs team is built to withstand the forces that undid those teams. “Because we don’t have no egos. They had strong egos in that locker room. Strong-ass egos,” Castle says, referring to that star-studded 2012 Thunder squad. “That’s why we’re so good,” Harper says. “We’ve got eight people on the team that, if we all had an ego, we wouldn’t blend together.”

Harper and Castle are discussing how short this offseason has felt for the pair when a smile erupts across Harper’s face.

“I’m going to win Sixth Man of the Year this year,” he says.

“No you’re not, bro,” Castle scoffs.

The reference—to the prize awarded to the best player who comes off the bench—is surprising; only a month earlier at a press conference after the Finals, teammate Devin Vassell suggested that Harper had been frustrated with “playing time and different roles that he was in.”

“I’m going to win Sixth Man of the Year,” Harper insists.

“You’re not going to be Sixth Man,” Castle says. “Who are you going to be Sixth Man for?”

“I don’t fucking know—God?” Harper answers.

You don’t actually think you’re going to come off the bench, do you? I cut in.

“What’s the political answer here?” Harper says, looking down at my recorder again. He calibrates his voice into its cheeriest pitch: “I’m going to do whatever the team needs me to do, man. If that’s come off the bench….”

He stops. “That’s crazy. Fuck no. I ain’t coming off no bench.”

“Bro, all you got to know is you going to be in the starting lineup,” Castle says, ending the discussion. “Be ready to hoop.” (Later in the conversation, Harper walks the Sixth Man thing back: “I was lying,” he says. “I had a smile on my face.”)

When I talk to Mitch Johnson in early August, I ask about the possibility that he’ll start Harper, and he answers in perfect coachspeak: “I don’t envision anybody being in the starting lineup yet,” he says, before adding, “Dylan and Steph will have very big roles.” However, he knows it’s only natural for any player in the league to be uncomfortable with anything but the biggest possible role. “I would hope that every player wants to make all the shots and to guard the best player and to play all the minutes and to score all the points and win all the games.”

Jacket by Jacquemus. Shirt by Wythe. T-shirt, his own. Pants by Amiri. Boots by Tecovas.

Fox has eagerly taken on the role of mentoring the young guards even though their ascension may come at the cost of his starting job. “I’m not worried about it at all,” the nine-year NBA vet says. “That’s not my decision to make. I go in, I control what I can control, and try to help put us in the best position to win.”

In Castle and Harper, you can see the early outlines of an all-time NBA pairing. “Even if Victor Wembanyama vanished,” Goldsberry says, “the Spurs, having these two dudes, still have one of the brightest futures in the league.”

Defining those early contours requires not just sorting out roles but also figuring out everything else that comes with being a star player in the league. The outfits, of course, have become increasingly essential. So much so that before a Finals game in New York, Harper and teammate Carter Bryant went shopping for outfits to wear to the game the next day. “We definitely went to Balenciaga, got a bunch of shit,” Harper says.

Despite playing until mid-June in the Finals, the two have already filled their calendars back up with basketball activities. Harper says it took his body weeks to feel normal again after the long playoff run, but lately he’s been working out, running stairs in Santa Barbara. He’ll head to Turks and Caicos this weekend with his brother—Celtics wing Ron Harper Jr.— while other teammates go to practice with Fox in Houston. In late July, they’ll travel to Paris for a Wembanyama-organized hangout that’s about as mandatory as an unofficial team event can be. “You want that max [contract extension] next year, you’ll be there,” Harper tells Castle, when the latter says he doesn’t have to attend.

Harper is already scheduled to be back in San Antonio for two weeks at the start of August. “They got you on that rookie plan,” Castle observes. Before long, training camp will ramp up. Another season, another shot for the two guards to meet their goals: to make the All-Star and All-Defensive teams, Castle says, and—they both say this nearly simultaneously—“Win a championship.”

Coat by Zegna. Shirt by Wythe. T-shirt, his own. Pants by Amiri. Boots by Tecovas. Belt by Stetson.

“I’m over it,” Harper says of the Finals. “You over it?” he turns to ask Castle.

When I ask if any moments from the series still haunt him, Harper fishes his phone out of his pocket to revisit one of the most painful beats, just to prove how over it he is: OG Anunoby’s tip-in from Game 4, which capped off a 29-point Knicks comeback, the largest in Finals history. As a fan, even a month later, watching this is like watching a character wander into the basement in a horror movie; I want to yell at him to stop.

As the Knicks dug their way out of the hole, Harper and Castle could feel the floor of Madison Square Garden quaking underneath their feet. “That’s the loudest I’ve ever heard an arena,” Harper says, scrubbing through an Instagram clip. He eventually finds the angle he’s looking for and points to his reaction under the basket, the O of his mouth growing in slow motion.

“That shit is hilarious,” Harper says.

“No,” Castle says, turning away, “I don’t be watching that shit, bro.”

“I got to watch it, bro. It happened,” Harper says.

It took Harper several weeks to wash the taste of the Finals loss out of his mouth, but it got easier when he restarted his workouts. “It helps me work out harder,” he says.

Every great team in NBA history has painful playoff series on their résumés; it’s a credit to this Spurs squad that theirs just happened to come in the Finals. Castle and Harper have put the loss behind them—“Just for the offseason, I’m over it,” Harper says—but they’re trying to take the necessary lessons from it, too. “I don’t think it’s like, ‘Oh shit, we made it there, it’s easy,’ ” Harper says. “It’s more that we understand what goes into [making] it. Now, we got to do it.”

I ask them to project out over the next five years. How many Finals appearances do they envision? “Hopefully five,” Harper says. “I mean, that’s the goal.”

Castle finishes his backcourt partner’s thought one more time: “We finna go back.”
